methods.title: Least-squares regression line → slope b and intercept a
methods.trigger: Paired measurements of two variables (or their sums Σx, Σy, Σx², Σxy) are given and the question asks for the regression line of the dependent variable on the independent variable.
formula: b=\frac{n\sum x_iy_i-\sum x_i\sum y_i}{n\sum x_i^2-(\sum x_i)^2}

methods.title: Scatter about the line → s_y|x, s_a and s_b
methods.trigger: The question asks for the residual (standard error of the estimate) SD about the regression line, or for the standard errors of the intercept and slope.

methods.title: Slope t test and CIs for β and α → significance of the trend
methods.trigger: The question asks whether there is a significant relationship (trend) between two variables, or asks for a confidence interval for the slope or intercept, by hand or from lm() output.

methods.title: Prediction at x → CI for the line of means vs CI for one observation
methods.trigger: The question asks for the mean of y at a given x with its confidence interval, or for the range expected for a single new individual at that x.

methods.title: Two regression lines → t test for a difference in slopes
methods.trigger: Two groups each have their own regression of y on x, and the question asks whether the slopes (or intercepts) differ.

methods.title: Pearson correlation r → strength of association and its t test
methods.trigger: The question asks how strongly two variables are associated, for the Pearson correlation coefficient, or whether the correlation differs from zero.

cases.title: Least-squares line for 10 Martians
cases.context: A random sample of 10 Martians is drawn from a population of 200. Height x (cm) and weight y (g) are recorded for each Martian, and the totals of x, y, x² and xy are formed as in Table 8-1.
tasks: Using the column totals, calculate the least-squares slope b and intercept a. Show the shared denominator, both numerators, and the check \(a=\bar y-b\bar x\).
Write the regression line and compare it with the population line of means \(\mu_{y|x}=-8+0.5x\).
cases.symbols: \(n\) (number of Martians), \(x\) (height, cm), \(y\) (weight, g), \(b\) (least-squares slope, g/cm), \(a\) (least-squares intercept, g), \(\bar x,\bar y\) (sample means), \(D\) (shared denominator).

steps.title: Collect the sums
steps.words: The least-squares formulas need only these five numbers, read from the bottom row of Table 8-1.

steps.title: Calculate the shared denominator
steps.words: Both the slope and the intercept formulas divide by this quantity, in cm².

steps.title: Calculate the slope
steps.words: The slope is the estimated increase in mean weight per centimeter of height, in g/cm.

steps.title: Calculate both sample means
steps.words: The least-squares line passes through the point of means (36.9 cm, 10.38 g).

steps.title: Calculate the intercept from the means
steps.words: Carry the unrounded slope into this step; rounding b to 0.44 first would move a to about −5.86 g.

steps.title: Check the intercept with the full formula
steps.words: Both routes give the same intercept, in grams.

steps.title: Write the line and compare with the line of means
steps.words: The sample line estimates the population line. Its slope 0.44 g/cm is near the true 0.5 g/cm, and the difference reflects which 10 Martians were sampled.

cases.conclusion: The least-squares line is \(\hat y=-6.008+0.4441x\) (slide: \(\hat y=-6.0+0.44x\)). Mean Martian weight is estimated to rise by about 0.44 g for each additional centimeter of height.

cases.title: Martian scatter about the line and coefficient standard errors
cases.context: For the same sample of 10 Martians, the slide summarizes the data with rounded values: the SD of height is 5.0 cm, the SD of weight is 2.4 g, the slope is 0.44 g/cm, and the mean height is 36.9 cm.
tasks: Estimate \(\sigma_{y|x}\) with the shortcut \(s_{y|x}=\sqrt{\frac{n-1}{n-2}(s_y^2-b^2s_x^2)}\).
Calculate the standard errors \(s_b\) and \(s_a\) from the formulas, and compare with the values from the unrounded raw data.
cases.symbols: \(s_{y|x}\) (standard error of the estimate, g), \(s_x,s_y\) (sample SDs), \(b\) (slope), \(s_b\) (SE of the slope, g/cm), \(s_a\) (SE of the intercept, g), \(\bar x\) (mean height), \(n\) (sample size).

steps.title: Square the pieces inside the shortcut
steps.words: The first term is the total variance of weight; the second is the part of it explained by the line.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the estimate
steps.words: The factor (n−1)/(n−2) converts the n−1 denominators of the sample variances into the n−2 denominator required for regression. The result, about 1.02 g, estimates the true σ_y|x = 1 g.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the slope
steps.words: Using the rounded 1.02 g instead gives 0.068 g/cm. The slide prints 0.064 g/cm, which matches the unrounded data (step 6).

steps.title: Evaluate the bracket for the intercept
steps.words: The second term is large because the mean height lies far from x = 0, where the intercept is defined.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the intercept
steps.words: With 1.02 g the result is 2.53 g; the slide prints 2.6 g. The intercept is far less precise than the slope because it is an extrapolation to zero height.

steps.title: Compare with the unrounded raw data
steps.words: From the ten observations and the unrounded line, the residual sum of squares is 7.438 g². The shortcut with rounded inputs overstates s_y|x because it subtracts two nearly equal numbers; R output reproduces the raw-data values.

cases.conclusion: From the slide's rounded inputs, \(s_{y|x}=1.017\) g (slide: 1.02 g), \(s_b=0.0678\) g/cm and \(s_a=2.52\) g. The unrounded data give 0.964 g, 0.0643 g/cm and 2.39 g.
cases.answerName: Standard error of the estimate s_y|x

cases.title: Is Martian weight related to height?
cases.context: The Martian sample of n = 10 gives the slope b = 0.44 g/cm with standard error s_b = 0.064 g/cm, and the intercept a = −6.0 g with standard error s_a = 2.6 g, as printed on the slides.
tasks: Test whether there is a relationship between height and weight at the 0.05 level. State the hypotheses, the statistic, the degrees of freedom and the printed critical value, and give the P range.
Construct the 95% confidence intervals for the slope β and for the intercept of the line of means.

hypotheses.nullWords: There is no linear relationship between height and weight in the Martian population: the slope of the line of means is zero.
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Mean Martian weight changes linearly with height: the slope of the line of means is not zero.

cases.symbols: \(b\) (sample slope), \(s_b\) (SE of the slope), \(a\) (sample intercept), \(s_a\) (SE of the intercept), \(\beta\) (population slope), \(\alpha_{LOM}\) (population intercept), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom), \(t_\alpha(\nu)\) (two-tailed critical value).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Use the t test for the slope of a regression line. The null states that mean Martian weight does not change with height.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: Under the null, β = 0, so the statistic is the slope divided by its standard error.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom
steps.words: Two coefficients were estimated from the data.

steps.title: Find the 0.05 critical value
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, two-tailed column 0.05. The printed cutoff is 2.306.

steps.title: Make the decision
steps.words: The statistic exceeds the cutoff, so the null hypothesis of no relationship is rejected.

steps.title: Find the P range
steps.words: Row 8, column 0.001 prints 5.041 (the slide writes 5.401). The statistic exceeds the largest printed cutoff, so P < 0.001.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the slope
steps.words: The interval excludes 0, which agrees with the test, and it contains the true slope 0.5 g/cm.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the intercept
steps.words: The intercept interval is wide and contains the true value −8 g.

cases.conclusion: t = 6.875 with ν = 8 exceeds t_0.05(8) = 2.306 and t_0.001(8) = 5.041, so the null is rejected (P < 0.001): Martian weight increases with height. The 95% CI for β is 0.2924 to 0.5876 g/cm, and for α_LOM it is −11.9956 to −0.0044 g.

cases.title: Martians 40 cm tall: mean weight and one Martian's weight
cases.context: Use the Martian regression \(\hat y=-6.0+0.44x\) with \(s_{y|x}=1.02\) g, n = 10, \(\bar x=36.9\) cm and \(s_x=5.0\) cm.
tasks: Construct the 95% confidence interval for the mean weight of Martians 40 cm tall (the line of means at x = 40).
Construct the 95% confidence interval for the weight of a single Martian 40 cm tall, and explain why it is wider.
cases.symbols: \(\hat y\) (predicted mean weight), \(s_{\hat y}\) (SE of the predicted mean), \(s_{Y_{new}}\) (SE for one new Martian), \(s_{y|x}\) (scatter about the line), \(\bar x\) (mean height), \(s_x\) (SD of height), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Calculate the predicted weight
steps.words: This is the estimated mean weight at 40 cm, in grams.

steps.title: Evaluate the distance term
steps.words: The second term grows with the distance between 40 cm and the mean height.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the mean prediction
steps.words: This standard error describes uncertainty in the height of the line at x = 40.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, column 0.05.

steps.title: Construct the interval for the mean
steps.words: With 95% confidence, the mean weight of all 40 cm Martians lies between about 10.71 and 12.49 g; the true mean is 12 g.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error for one new Martian
steps.words: Add the individual scatter about the line to the uncertainty in the line itself. The same value follows from 1.02√(1+0.1427111).

steps.title: Construct the interval for one Martian
steps.words: This interval should contain the weight of a single randomly chosen Martian 40 cm tall with 95% confidence.

steps.title: Compare the two widths
steps.words: The observation interval is about 2.8 times as wide, because individual Martians scatter about the mean with SD near 1 g even if the line were known exactly.

cases.conclusion: 95% CI for the mean weight at 40 cm: 10.71144 to 12.48856 g. 95% CI for one Martian's weight at 40 cm: 9.085639 to 14.11436 g.
cases.answerName: Lower endpoint of the mean-weight CI

cases.title: Martian correlation coefficient and its t test
cases.context: Table 8-3 gives, for the 10 sampled Martians, the totals of the deviation products and squared deviations from the means.
tasks: Calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient r and check it with the slope relation.
Test whether the correlation differs from zero at the 0.05 level, and give the P range.

hypotheses.nullWords: There is no linear relationship between height and weight in the Martian population (the population correlation is zero).
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Height and weight are linearly related in the Martian population (the population correlation is not zero).

cases.symbols: \(r\) (sample correlation coefficient), \(\rho\) (population correlation), \(b\) (slope), \(n\) (number of pairs), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: Calculate r from the deviation totals
steps.words: The units g·cm cancel, so r has no units. The slide rounds to 0.925.

steps.title: Check with the slope relation
steps.words: The deviation form of the slope equals the n·Σxy formula, and r has the same sign as b.

steps.title: Square r
steps.words: About 86% of the variation in weight is accounted for by the linear relationship with height.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: This matches the slope statistic b/s_b computed from the same data (6.907 from the unrounded data).

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and the 0.05 cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 8, two-tailed column 0.05.

steps.title: Decide and give the P range
steps.words: Reject the null hypothesis of zero correlation.

steps.title: Interpret r
steps.words: A value this close to +1 indicates a strong positive linear relationship: taller Martians tend to be heavier.

cases.conclusion: r = 0.9256 (slide: 0.925). t = 6.915 with ν = 8 exceeds 5.041, so the correlation differs from zero (P < 0.001).

cases.title: Male Plutonians: intervals, correlation and predictions at 68 inches
cases.context: For 18 male Plutonians, lm(Weight.lbs ~ Height.in) gives the coefficients below, a residual standard error of 2.711 lb on 16 degrees of freedom, and multiple R-squared 0.9418. The heights in the data table total 1215 in, with Σx² = 82,189 in².
tasks: Give the standard errors of \(b_0\) and \(b_1\) and their 95% confidence intervals.
Give the correlation coefficient.
Give the mean weight of a male 68 inches tall, the 95% CI for that mean, and the 95% CI for the weight of one male 68 inches tall.
cases.symbols: \(b_0=a\) (intercept, lb), \(b_1=b\) (slope, lb/in), \(s_a,s_b\) (standard errors), \(s_{y|x}\) (residual standard error), \(R^2\) (multiple R-squared), \(\bar x,s_x\) (mean and SD of height), \(s_{\hat y},s_{Y_{new}}\) (SEs for the mean and for one male).

steps.title: Read the coefficients and standard errors
steps.words: The Std. Error column answers part (a) directly.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom and cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 16, two-tailed column 0.05.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the slope
steps.words: Each additional inch adds between about 2.85 and 3.72 lb to mean male weight; the interval excludes 0.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the intercept
steps.words: The interval contains 0, matching Pr(>|t|) = 0.763. The intercept is an extrapolation to zero height.

steps.title: Calculate the correlation coefficient
steps.words: The slope is positive, so r is positive.

steps.title: Predict the mean weight at 68 inches
steps.words: This answers part (d), in pounds.

steps.title: Find the mean and SD of height
steps.words: These come from the height column of the data table.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for the mean at 68 inches
steps.words: 68 inches is close to the mean height, so the mean is estimated precisely.

steps.title: Construct the 95% interval for one male at 68 inches
steps.words: The interval for one male is more than four times as wide as the interval for the mean.

cases.answerName: Lower endpoint of the mean-weight CI at 68 in

cases.title: Male versus female Plutonians: comparing slopes
cases.context: Separate regressions of weight (lb) on height (in) were fitted to 18 male and 18 female Plutonians with lm(). Female heights total 1138 in with Σx² = 72,200 in², giving a mean of 63.22 in and an SD of 3.859 in.
tasks: Test whether the slopes of the male and female lines of means differ at the 0.05 level. State the hypotheses in words, the statistic, ν, the printed critical value and the P range.
Apply the corresponding test to the intercepts.

hypotheses.nullWords: Weight increases with height at the same rate in male and female Plutonians (equal slopes of the two lines of means).
hypotheses.alternativeWords: The rate at which weight increases with height differs between male and female Plutonians.

cases.symbols: \(b_M,b_F\) (male and female slopes), \(s_{b_M},s_{b_F}\) (their SEs), \(s_{b_M-b_F}\) (SE of the slope difference), \(a_M,a_F\) (intercepts), \(\nu\) (degrees of freedom).

steps.title: State the procedure and hypotheses
steps.words: Use the two-regression-line t test. Both slopes were significant on their own (t = 16.088 and 4.309), so the comparison is meaningful.

steps.title: Calculate the slope difference
steps.words: Keep the order males minus females throughout.

steps.title: Calculate the standard error of the difference
steps.words: The equal-n formula applies because both groups have 18 points.

steps.title: Calculate the t statistic
steps.words: The difference is about 2.4 standard errors.

steps.title: Find the degrees of freedom
steps.words: Each line uses up two degrees of freedom for its intercept and slope.

steps.title: Compare with the 0.05 cutoff
steps.words: Open t_table.pdf, PDF page 1, row 32, two-tailed column 0.05. Reject equal slopes.

steps.title: Find the P range
steps.words: The statistic lies between the 0.05 and 0.02 columns of row 32.

steps.title: Apply the corresponding intercept test
steps.words: Replacing slopes by intercepts in the same formula gives |t| = 0.337 < 2.037, so the intercepts do not differ significantly. The intercepts are extrapolations to zero height with very large standard errors.

cases.conclusion: t = 2.444 with ν = 32 exceeds t_0.05(32) = 2.037 but not t_0.02(32) = 2.449, so the slopes differ (0.02 < P < 0.05): male weight rises faster with height (3.28 lb/in) than female weight (2.03 lb/in).

cases.title: Caffeine dose and finger-tapping rate (by hand from sums)
cases.context: Original practice example (invented numbers, not from the lecture or homework). Forty-five volunteers each receive a caffeine dose x (mg, 0 to 300) and then perform a finger-tapping test; y is taps per 10 s. Only the sums are given, and R is not to be used.
tasks: Find the regression line of tapping rate on dose.
Calculate \(s_a\), \(s_b\) and the estimate of the variance about the line of means, \(s_{y|x}^2\).
Using b, test whether the trend is significant at the 0.05 level.
Construct the 95% CI for the mean tapping rate at 200 mg, and the 95% CI for one volunteer's tapping rate at 200 mg.
Calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient.

hypotheses.nullWords: Mean tapping rate does not change linearly with caffeine dose (the slope of the line of means is zero).
hypotheses.alternativeWords: Mean tapping rate changes linearly with caffeine dose (the slope of the line of means is not zero).

cases.symbols: \(x\) (dose, mg), \(y\) (taps per 10 s), \(S_{xx},S_{yy},S_{xy}\) (sums of squared and cross deviations), \(s_x,s_y\) (sample SDs), \(s_{y|x}\) (scatter about the line), \(s_a,s_b\) (SEs of the coefficients), \(s_{\hat y},s_{Y_{new}}\) (SEs for the mean and for one volunteer), \(r\) (correlation).

steps.title: Calculate both means
steps.words: These are the coordinates of the point the regression line passes through.

steps.title: Calculate the deviation sums
steps.words: These equal Σ(x−x̄)², Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) and Σ(y−ȳ)².

steps.title: Calculate the slope
general: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}
steps.words: Equivalently b = S_xy/S_xx = 15336.4/338720. Tapping rate rises by about 0.045 taps per 10 s per mg.

steps.title: Calculate the intercept
steps.words: The line is ŷ = 50.80 + 0.04528x.

steps.title: Calculate the sample variances
steps.words: These feed the shortcut formula for s_y|x.

steps.title: Estimate the variance about the line of means
steps.words: This is the requested estimate of the variance of the line of means, in (taps/10 s)².

steps.title: Calculate the coefficient standard errors
steps.words: Note (n−1)s_x² = S_xx = 338720.

steps.title: Calculate t and bracket the missing table row
steps.words: Row 43 is not printed. Bracket it with rows 42 and 44 on PDF page 1 and use the conservative row-42 cutoff 2.018 (the two rows differ by only 0.003).

steps.title: Decide and give the P range
steps.words: t exceeds both bracketing 0.001 cutoffs, so the trend is significant with P < 0.001.

steps.title: Construct the 95% CI for the mean at 200 mg
steps.words: Using the row-44 value 2.015 would move the lower bound only to 58.3309.

steps.title: Construct the 95% CI for one volunteer at 200 mg
steps.words: The single-observation interval is much wider because it includes the person-to-person scatter.

steps.title: Calculate the correlation coefficient
steps.words: A moderate positive correlation. Its t statistic equals b/s_b, so the correlation test agrees with the slope test.

cases.answerName: Lower endpoint of the mean CI at 200 mg

sampleQuestions.stem: Using the column totals for the 10 Martians, what is the least-squares slope b?
sampleQuestions.why: The slope is (10·3930.1 − 369·103.8)/(10·13841 − 369²) = 998.8/2249 = 0.4441 g/cm. The value 0.5 g/cm is the population slope, which the sample only estimates.
equations: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}

sampleQuestions.stem: What is the least-squares intercept a for the Martian sample?
sampleQuestions.why: With the unrounded slope, a = ȳ − b x̄ = 10.38 − 0.4441(36.9) = −6.008 g. Rounding b to 0.44 first gives −5.856 g, and adding instead of subtracting gives 26.77 g.

sampleQuestions.stem: Using the slide's rounded values, what is the standard error of the estimate \(s_{y|x}\)?
sampleQuestions.why: s_y|x = √[(9/8)(5.76 − 4.84)] = √1.035 = 1.017 g. Forgetting the root gives 1.035, dropping the 9/8 factor gives 0.959, and inverting it gives 0.904.

sampleQuestions.stem: With \(s_{y|x}=1.017\) g and \(s_x=5.0\) cm, what is the standard error of the slope \(s_b\)?
sampleQuestions.why: s_b = (1/√9)(1.017/5.0) = 0.0678 g/cm. Omitting 1/√(n−1) gives 0.2035, dividing by 9 instead of 3 gives 0.0226, and using s_x² gives 0.0136.

sampleQuestions.stem: With \(s_{y|x}=1.017\) g, what is the standard error of the intercept \(s_a\) for the Martians?
sampleQuestions.why: s_a = 1.017√(0.1 + 36.9²/(9·25)) = 1.017√6.1516 = 2.523 g. Dropping the x̄² term gives 0.322, skipping the root gives 6.258, and dropping 1/n gives 2.503.

sampleQuestions.stem: What is the t statistic for testing \(H_0:\beta=0\) with b = 0.44 g/cm and \(s_b=0.064\) g/cm?
sampleQuestions.why: t = b/s_b = 0.44/0.064 = 6.875. Using the population slope 0.5 in the numerator would give 7.813, which is not the null value.

sampleQuestions.stem: Which printed two-tailed value is \(t_{0.001}(8)\) in the course t table?
sampleQuestions.why: Row 8, column 0.001 prints 5.041. The slide writes 5.401, a transposition; 4.781 is row 9 and 3.355 is the 0.01 column.

sampleQuestions.stem: What is the lower endpoint of the 95% confidence interval for the Martian slope β?
sampleQuestions.why: 0.44 − 2.306(0.064) = 0.2924 g/cm with ν = 8. Using ν = 10 (2.228) gives 0.2974, using 1.96 gives 0.3146, and using the 0.001 cutoff gives 0.1174.
